reason: Point 3.6.1 does not mandate a full root-cause review for every minor security event regardless of relevance or feasibility. Broadening the requirement to all minor events and eliminating standard conditionality constitutes a material distortion.

The claim introduces an absolute obligation ('compulsory following every minor security event, regardless of relevance or feasibility'), thereby removing the essential conditionality ('where appropriate', 'where possible') set out in the Annex point.
Point 7.2 requires entities to determine appropriate assessment methods taking into account previous significant incidents, directly contradicting the claim that they need not be considered.

The claim contradicts point 7.2, which requires entities to take into account past significant incidents, alongside risk assessment results, when establishing processes to assess the effectiveness of cybersecurity risk-management measures.

The claim broadens Annex point 3.6.1 to every minor security event and removes proportionality/feasibility. The provision concerns root-cause analysis in incident handling, not an unconditional full review after all minor events.

Annex point 7.2 requires previous significant cybersecurity incidents to be considered when choosing how to assess security-control effectiveness. The claim reverses that requirement by saying they need not be considered, which is a material legal distortion.

Point 2.3.2 of the Annex permits independent reviews to be performed by qualified internal staff, provided they are independent of the audited area, including not being in the reporting chain of the audited area.

The claim accurately reflects point 2.3.2 of the Annex, which allows independent reviews to be conducted by competent internal staff provided they are not in the reporting chain of the area being audited.

Point 2.3.2 permits an internal independent review to be performed by qualified internal staff provided they are not in the reporting chain of the audited area; the claim tracks that condition without material broadening.

Point 3.1.1 requires incident-handling policies and procedures to cover the full incident lifecycle, including detection, containment, analysis, response, recovery, and reporting. Limiting the policy solely to authority notifications and making detection and recovery optional is a material legal distortion.

The claim misrepresents the requirement by asserting that internal detection and recovery procedures are optional; point 3.1.1 mandates procedures covering detection, analysis, containment/response, recovery, and documentation alongside reporting.

Point 3.1.1 requires an incident-handling policy covering detection, analysis, containment, recovery and notification; it does not make internal detection and recovery procedures optional or limit the policy to notifying authorities.

Point 2.1.4 of the Annex requires that results of risk assessments and risk treatment plans be reviewed and updated at planned intervals (at least annually), following a significant incident, or following major changes to the risk environment or systems.

The requirement faithfully reflects point 2.1.4 of the Annex, which mandates reviewing risk assessment results and risk treatment plans at least annually and following significant incidents or operational/risk changes.
No source text for Annex point 2.1.4 was provided, so I cannot verify whether it requires annual review plus significant incidents or major risk changes; abstaining rather than inferring.

The claim accurately reflects Point 7.2 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires procedures assessing the effectiveness of cybersecurity risk-management measures to take into account relevant risk assessments and previous significant incidents, and to specify roles and responsibilities for carrying out measurements.

The claim accurately reflects point 7.2 of the Annex, which requires procedures for assessing the effectiveness of cybersecurity risk-management measures to take into account risk assessments and prior significant incidents, including assigning measurement responsibilities.

Point 7.2 requires effectiveness-assessment policies/procedures to specify measurement responsibilities and take into account relevant risk assessments and previous significant incidents. The proposed requirement accurately summarizes those elements without material distortion.
Point 2.1.1 requires that residual risks be formally accepted by appropriate management levels and documented, rather than accepted by any team member without management reporting.

The claim materially distorts the requirement; residual risks cannot be accepted by arbitrary project team members and explicitly require acceptance by management or properly authorized accountable persons, along with management reporting.

Point 2.1.1 does not permit any project team member to accept residual cybersecurity risks without management involvement. Residual-risk acceptance must be governed by an approved risk-management policy and subject to management approval/reporting, so the proposed requirement materially removes oversight and delegation controls.

The claim contradicts the core principles of access control in point 11.2.2, which mandate restricting access rights based on the principle of least privilege and need-to-know, rather than granting broad privileged access by default.

Point 11.2.2(a) requires access rights management to adhere to the principles of need-to-know, least privilege, and separation of duties. Granting broad privileged access by default until misuse occurs directly contradicts the requirement of least privilege.

The claim materially distorts Annex point 11.2.2(a): it converts access control into a default of broad privileged access for all staff and invents a post-misuse trigger. The provision requires restricted, justified access rights, not blanket privileged access pending misuse.

Point 2.3.2 of the Annex requires internal reviews and audits to be objective, impartial, and independent. Permitting a manager to review their own directly reporting team introduces an inherent conflict of interest, directly contradicting the requirement that reviewers must be independent of the operational activities and teams they assess.

The claim directly contradicts point 2.3.2, which requires independent reviews to be conducted by individuals who are independent of the area being reviewed, meaning internal reviewers must be outside the reporting authority of personnel in the assessed area.

Point 2.3.2 requires reviews to be independent of the activity reviewed. A manager reviewing their own directly reporting team is not independent, so the claim's 'always permitted' wording removes a material conditionality.
Point 4.2.3 requires entities to periodically test and verify the integrity and restorability of backups. Storing backups off-site does not exempt entities from conducting backup integrity checks.
The claim introduces an unauthorized exemption. Point 4.2.3 requires relevant entities to regularly verify backup-copy integrity regardless of whether backups are stored off-site.

Annex point 4.2.3 requires backup integrity/availability to be verified; off-site storage does not eliminate that obligation. The claim removes a required control and is therefore a material distortion.

The claim accurately reflects point 4.2.3 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires relevant entities to carry out regular integrity checks of their backup copies without adding unauthorized constraints or altering scope.
The claim accurately reflects the requirement under point 4.2.3 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which mandates that relevant entities regularly check the integrity of their backup copies.
Point 4.2.3 requires regular testing/verification of backup integrity. The claim restates that requirement as a compliance measure without broadening scope or adding conditions.

The claim accurately reflects point 6.4.3 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires emergency changes bypassing standard procedures to be documented, including the details of what changed and the justification for utilizing the emergency procedure.
The claim accurately reflects point 6.4.3, which requires relevant entities to document the outcome of emergency changes and the justification for not following standard change procedures.

Point 6.4.3 requires emergency changes that bypass routine change procedures to be documented, including what changed and why the normal process could not be followed. The proposed requirement faithfully summarizes that obligation.

Point 3.1.1 requires relevant entities to establish and implement an incident-handling policy and procedures covering the incident-handling lifecycle (such as detection, containment, recovery, and communication), defining roles and responsibilities, and ensuring timely reporting. The claim accurately reflects these elements as a non-exhaustive summary.

The claim accurately reflects the core obligations of point 3.1.1 of the Annex, requiring an incident-handling policy to allocate responsibilities and define handling processes, non-exhaustively covering detection, containment, recovery, and reporting.

The claim is a faithful, non-exhaustive summary of Annex point 3.1.1: an incident-handling policy is expected to define response roles and processes, including detection, containment, recovery and reporting. 'Timely' does not materially distort the provision.

Point 8.2.4 mandates cybersecurity awareness, education, and training on a regular basis, including when roles change or new threats arise, directly contradicting the claim that training is only for new hires and never upon role changes.

The claim materially distorts the requirement by stating training is never required upon changing roles, whereas point 8.2.4 requires that personnel moving into roles demanding security-relevant competencies receive appropriate cybersecurity training.

Point 8.2.4 does not limit cybersecurity training to newly hired personnel; it also covers role changes and other personnel circumstances. The claim narrows the scope and adds an absolute prohibition, materially distorting the Annex provision.

Point 2.1.1 of the Annex explicitly provides that residual cybersecurity risks may be formally accepted by accountable, authorised risk owners, provided that the management body receives adequate reporting on those residual risks.

The claim accurately reflects the requirements of point 2.1.1, which permits authorized accountable risk owners to accept residual cybersecurity risks provided the management body receives appropriate reporting.

The claim mirrors point 2.1.1: residual risks may be accepted by accountable risk owners authorised for that purpose, with reporting to the management body; it does not omit a material condition or broaden scope.
Point 6.4.3 requires that emergency changes be documented, tested retrospectively, and reviewed and approved after implementation. They are not exempt from post-change documentation.

The claim contradicts point 6.4.3, which requires entities to document the result of emergency changes and the reasons normal procedures could not be followed, rather than exempting them from documentation.

Point 6.4.3 may allow emergency changes to bypass normal approval steps, but it does not exempt them from all post-change documentation. The claim broadens the exception and removes the likely retrospective documentation/review condition, creating a material legal distortion.

Point 1.2.3 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 directly requires relevant entities to assign at least one person to report directly to the management body on network and information security matters.

The claim accurately reflects point 1.2.3(a) of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires relevant entities to assign at least one person who reports directly to the management body on the security of network and information systems.
Faithful to Annex point 1.2.3: it requires at least one person to report directly to the management body on cybersecurity/NIS matters. The claim adds no deadline or material broadening.
Point 3.5.5 does not require incident response procedures to be tested once every 24 hours. Requiring daily testing is an invented and unrealistic frequency, representing a material legal distortion.

Point 3.5.5 does not require incident response procedures to be tested every 24 hours; testing is required at planned intervals or following significant changes, making the daily testing requirement an invented deadline.

Annex point 3.5.5 does not impose a 24-hour testing frequency for all incident response procedures. The proposed daily deadline is an invented, materially stricter obligation than the provision requires.

Without the verified source text for point 10.2.1 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, it cannot be confirmed whether background verification obligations apply to direct suppliers or service providers under this specific point or whether it pertains to other human resources security requirements.
The claim accurately reflects point 10.2.1, properly preserving the conditional qualifiers regarding feasibility, necessity for the role, and applicability to direct suppliers and service providers.

The requirement tracks Annex point 10.2.1: background verification is conditioned on feasibility and role necessity and extends to employees and applicable direct suppliers or service providers. No material distortion.

Point 1.2.3 requires direct reporting lines to the management body specifically for the designated role or person responsible for information security (e.g., CISO equivalent), not for every employee working in IT security. Broadening this requirement to all IT security staff is a material distortion.

Point 1.2.3 requires that at least one person reports directly to the management body regarding network and information system security. Extending this direct reporting obligation to every IT security employee is a material broadening of the legal scope.

Point 1.2.3 does not require every IT security employee to report directly to the management body. The claim materially broadens the Annex provision, which concerns management-body governance/accountability rather than a universal direct-reporting line for all IT security staff.

Point 13.1.2 does not mandate the installation of a fuel-powered emergency generator for all entities regardless of risk. Measures under the regulation are risk-based and proportionate, focusing on power and environmental protection measures appropriate to identified risks rather than prescribing specific hardware unconditionally.

The claim removes conditionality and imposes an absolute mandate. Point 13.1.2 requires entities to protect equipment against disruptions of supporting utilities where appropriate based on risk, rather than mandating a fuel-powered generator for every entity regardless of circumstances.

The claim materially broadens Annex point 13.1.2 by making a fuel-powered emergency generator mandatory for every relevant entity, regardless of risk exposure or operational circumstances. The provision is risk-based/conditional and does not impose such an unconditional requirement.

Point 10.2.1 does not require identical background checks for all personnel regardless of feasibility or role. Background verification checks must be proportional to business requirements, information classification, and perceived risks, and carried out in accordance with applicable laws.

The claim removes key conditionalities established in point 10.2.1. Background verification is required only to the extent feasible and where necessary according to roles, responsibilities, and authorisations, rather than unconditionally and identically for everyone.

The claim materially distorts point 10.2.1 by imposing identical checks on every employee and subcontractor regardless of feasibility, role, risk, proportionality, or legal conditions. It broadens scope and removes conditionality, so it is not a faithful compliance requirement.

The claim accurately reflects point 5.2.1(a) of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires entities to maintain an up-to-date list of direct suppliers and service providers, including their contact information and the relevant ICT products, services, or processes provided.

The claim accurately reflects point 5.2.1 of the Annex, which requires relevant entities to maintain an up-to-date list or registry of direct suppliers and service providers, including their contact information and the provided ICT products, services, or processes.

Point 5.2.1 requires an up-to-date register/list of direct suppliers and service providers, including contact details and relevant ICT services or offerings. The proposed requirement is a faithful, non-distorting summary.

Point 5.2.1 does not require organisations to record every indirect subcontractor of every supplier without exception. Supply chain documentation focuses on direct suppliers and critical or relevant subcontractors based on risk, making the claim an impermissible broadening of scope.
The requirement in point 5.2.1 mandates maintaining a registry of direct suppliers and service providers, not an exhaustive register of every indirect subcontractor.
No source text for Annex point 5.2.1 was provided, so I cannot verify whether the register must cover every indirect subcontractor without exception. Abstaining rather than inventing the provision.

Point 6.2.1 requires entities to establish and apply secure development rules across the entire lifecycle of network and information systems, including requirements and design/architecture, rather than restricting them exclusively to the final testing stage.

Point 6.2.1 applies secure development rules across the entire lifecycle, explicitly covering specification, design, development, implementation, and testing, rather than restricting them exclusively to the final testing stage.

Point 6.2.1 requires secure development rules across the development lifecycle, including requirements and architecture/design stages, not solely final testing. Limiting scope to final testing materially distorts the provision.

Point 1.1.2 requires the network and information security policy to be reviewed at planned intervals and specifically following significant incidents or substantial changes, directly contradicting the claim that reviews are only needed every five years even after significant incidents.

The claim introduces an incorrect review timeline of once every five years and falsely eliminates the requirement to review the policy following significant incidents, directly contradicting point 1.1.2.

Annex point 1.1.2 does not permit a five-year review cycle or dispense with review after significant incidents. The claim materially distorts the required review frequency and removes incident-driven conditionality.
Point 8.2.4 explicitly mandates that relevant entities provide appropriate cybersecurity training to personnel transferring to roles that require cybersecurity-relevant expertise.

The requirement faithfully reflects point 8.2.4 of the Annex, which mandates that the cybersecurity education and training programme provides relevant training to staff transferring to roles requiring cybersecurity competencies and expertise.
The claim faithfully reflects Annex point 8.2.4: training must cover personnel who transfer into roles requiring cybersecurity-relevant expertise. No material broadening or removal of conditionality.

Point 2.1.4 requires entities to regularly review and update their cybersecurity risk assessments, particularly following significant changes or security incidents, not solely upon first entering the scope of the regulation.

The claim introduces an incorrect limitation by asserting that risk assessment refreshes occur only when an entity first enters scope, directly contradicting the requirement to review risk assessments at planned intervals, at least annually, and following significant incidents or operational changes.

Annex point 2.1.4 requires risk assessments to be reviewed/refreshed periodically and when significant changes occur, not only when an entity first enters scope. The claim materially narrows the obligation.

The requirement faithfully reflects point 11.7.1 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires that, where appropriate, users authenticate using multi-factor authentication or continuous authentication mechanisms based on the classification of the asset accessed.

The proposed requirement accurately reflects Annex point 11.7.1, preserving the conditionality ('where appropriate') and the requirement for multi-factor or continuous authentication based on asset classification.

The proposed requirement tracks Annex point 11.7.1: it preserves the 'where appropriate' condition, allows multi-factor or continuous authentication, and requires account to be taken of the accessed asset's classification.

Point 9.1 of the Annex does not prescribe a specific cipher such as AES-256, nor does it mandate blanket encryption regardless of classification or risk. The regulation requires establishing and maintaining cryptography policies based on risk assessments and data classification.

Point 9.1 requires cryptography policies and procedures based on risk assessments and asset classifications; it does not mandate a specific standard like AES-256 across all data and devices regardless of risk.

Annex point 9.1 requires appropriate cryptographic and encryption measures, typically risk-based and subject to classification/state-of-the-art considerations. It does not mandate AES-256 universally for every dataset, device, and communication channel. The claim materially broadens scope and invents a specific algorithm.

The claim faithfully reflects the obligation under point 3.5.5 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires relevant entities to test their incident response procedures at planned intervals.
Point 3.5.5 requires relevant entities to test incident response procedures at planned intervals. The claim accurately reflects this requirement without introducing material distortions.
Point 3.5.5 requires incident response procedures to be tested at planned intervals. The claim’s wording 'defined, planned intervals' is consistent and adds no material deadline or scope distortion.

Point 9.1 of the Annex requires that the policy and rules on the use of cryptographic controls and mechanisms be based on and take into account the organisation's cybersecurity risk assessment and the classification of assets and information systems.

The claim accurately reflects point 9.1 of the Annex, which requires the choice and implementation of cryptography and encryption to be based on the entity's asset classification and cybersecurity risk assessment.

Point 9.1 links the choice and use of cryptography to the organisation's cybersecurity risk assessment and asset classification; the proposed requirement mirrors that linkage without adding deadlines or broadening scope.

The claim accurately reflects the obligations in point 3.6.1 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires entities, where appropriate, to conduct post-incident reviews following recovery and document lessons learned to mitigate future incidents.

The claim accurately reflects the obligations under point 3.6.1 of the Annex, properly preserving the conditionality ('where appropriate') and the requirement to conduct post-incident reviews and document lessons learned to mitigate future incident impacts.

Point 3.6.1 requires post-incident reviews after recovery and documentation of lessons learned, where appropriate, to reduce future incident impact. The proposed requirement faithfully tracks that obligation without material distortion.

Point 6.2.1 requires relevant entities to establish and apply rules for secure development throughout the software and systems development lifecycle, covering both in-house developments and outsourced developments.
The claim accurately reflects point 6.2.1, which mandates rules for secure development across the entire lifecycle, encompassing both in-house and outsourced development.
Point 6.2.1 requires secure development practices across the development lifecycle and covers internally developed and outsourced systems; the claim is a faithful, non-exhaustive summary.

The regulation does not impose a blanket requirement to completely remediate every discovered vulnerability within 24 hours regardless of criticality; this introduces an invented deadline and broadens the compliance scope.

The claim introduces an invented 24-hour deadline and broadens the scope to all vulnerabilities irrespective of criticality, whereas the regulation requires addressing vulnerabilities critical to operations without undue delay.
The claim invents an exact 24-hour deadline and applies it to every vulnerability regardless of criticality. Annex point 6.10.2(c) does not support such a blanket, non-risk-based remediation rule.

The claim accurately reflects point 13.1.2 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires entities to implement appropriate measures to protect against risks resulting from failures of utilities, including electricity and telecommunications.

The requirement faithfully reflects point 13.1.2 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires entities to protect equipment against disruptions caused by failures in supporting utilities, including electricity and telecommunications, maintaining appropriate conditionality without distortions.

The proposed requirement is a faithful paraphrase of Annex point 13.1.2, which calls for suitable safeguards for utility service availability/resilience, as appropriate, against electricity, telecommunications, water, or other utility risks. Omission of water as an example is not a material distortion because the provision uses non-exhaustive examples.

Point 1.1.2 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 requires the management body to review the policy on network and information systems security at least once every two years, or following a significant incident or change, rather than at least once per year. Substituting an annual cadence for the biennial requirement is a material legal distortion.

The requirement accurately reflects point 1.1.2 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which mandates that the policy be reviewed at least annually, following significant incidents or changes, and that the review be documented.

Point 1.1.2 requires review at least annually and upon significant changes, recording the outcome. The proposed requirement adds 'significant incidents' as a separate mandatory trigger, broadening the obligation beyond the Annex and creating a material legal distortion.

Point 11.7.1 mandates multi-factor authentication (which is not restricted to exactly two factors) based on risk assessments, specifically targeting sensitive systems, privileged access, or remote access, rather than imposing universal, unconditional application to every login across all information systems without exception.

The claim introduces material distortions by removing conditionality ('where appropriate', 'considering asset classification') and mandating an absolute rule ('every login', 'no asset-based exceptions') restricted to exactly two factors, whereas the regulation permits multi-factor or continuous authentication based on risk and asset classification.

Annex point 11.7.1 requires multi-factor authentication for access in relevant contexts; it does not mandate 'exactly two' factors for every login to every information system, nor an absolute no-exception rule. The claim materially broadens and rigidifies the obligation.

Without access to the definitive text of point 6.10.2(c) of the Annex to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, it cannot be confirmed whether point 6.10 exists or whether addressing operational critical vulnerabilities 'without undue delay' accurately reflects the specific legal obligations and conditions set out therein.

The claim faithfully reflects point 6.10.2(c) of the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which requires addressing vulnerabilities identified as critical to operations without undue delay without introducing unmandated rigid deadlines.

The proposal tracks Annex point 6.10.2(c): critical vulnerabilities must be handled without undue delay. 'Addressed' is a non-material paraphrase of the remediation/handling obligation and does not invent a deadline or broaden scope.

The claim accurately reflects point 11.2.2(a) of the Annex, which requires access rights allocation, modification, and revocation to adhere to the principles of least privilege, need-to-know, and segregation of duties.

The claim accurately reflects point 11.2.2(a) of the Annex, which requires access rights allocation and revocation to adhere to the principles of need-to-know, least privilege, and segregation of duties.

No Annex text was supplied, so I cannot verify whether point 11.2.2(a) expressly includes segregation of duties alongside least privilege and need-to-know, or whether the claim broadens the provision.
